topics.title: Python
topics.outcome: Write programs from print and input up to functions, collections, files, exceptions, modules, classes and unit tests.
topics.description: This topic assumes no programming experience. It climbs in three stages: Programs (steps 1–9). print, variables, types, input, operators, strings, if, while and for. You write whole programs; the tests run them with sample input and compare what they print. Functions and collections (steps 10–18). def, lists, comprehensions, dictionaries, tuples, the standard library, sets, functions as values and grouping records. From here on, tests call your functions and check their return values. Robust programs (steps 19–27). Raising exceptions, validating nested lists, handling exceptions, a stateful game loop, files and JSON, scripts that read standard input, classes, inheritance and writing your own unit tests. Packages: standard library only. Where Python has a built-in shortcut (sum, collections.Counter, math.comb), the lesson first shows the loop it replaces. Project ideas: ungraded briefs between steps suggest things to build with what you have learned so far.

topics.title: Mathematics for AI/ML
topics.outcome: Use summation, exponentials, logarithms, the sigmoid, vectors, matrices, derivatives, the chain rule, integration, gradient descent, series and eigenvectors.
topics.description: The mathematics that later topics use, each idea implemented in plain Python before NumPy appears. It starts with notation (Σ and Π), exponentials and logarithms, and the sigmoid — the pieces needed for probabilities and logistic regression — then moves through vectors and matrices, counting, small linear systems, numerical and analytic derivatives (including the chain rule used by backpropagation), integration, gradient descent, series and eigenvectors. Packages: standard library only. Each lesson compares the hand-written version with the math module where one exists; NP-02 and NP-06 later redo these operations in NumPy and check that the answers agree. Project ideas: ungraded briefs between steps suggest things to build with what you have learned so far.

topics.title: Statistics
topics.outcome: Describe data, reason with probability, conditional probability and Bayes' rule, use the binomial and normal distributions, simulate, and run interval estimates and hypothesis tests by hand and with scipy.stats.
topics.description: Describing data first (mean, variance, median, percentiles, histograms, z-scores), then probability (sample spaces, conditional probability, Bayes' rule), two named distributions (binomial and normal), simulation and the law of large numbers, correlation, sampling distributions and standard errors, and bootstrap intervals. The topic ends with scipy.stats: distribution objects, then the chi-square test, Welch's t-test and the permutation test, each followed by an optional deep dive that computes the same test by hand. Packages: standard library, then scipy for the last four required steps. Random simulations use random.Random(seed).random(), whose sequence Python documents as reproducible. Project ideas: an A/B test analyser and a dice-and-coin simulator.

topics.title: NumPy
topics.outcome: Replace Python loops with arrays: vectorised arithmetic, slicing, masks, reductions, matrix products, broadcasting, reshaping, gathers, seeded randomness and linear algebra.
topics.description: NumPy replaces Python loops over numbers with operations on whole arrays. The topic starts by creating and inspecting arrays and repeating the loops you wrote in Mathematics as vectorised expressions, then covers slicing, masks, axis reductions, matrix products, broadcasting, reshaping, gathers, seeded random generators, pairwise distances, linear solvers, one-hot encoding and sliding windows. Packages: numpy (validated on 2.2 and 2.5). Most tests check a NumPy implementation against a plain-Python reference so you can see they compute the same thing. Project ideas: ungraded briefs between steps suggest things to build with what you have learned so far.

topics.title: Pandas
topics.outcome: Load, inspect, clean, filter, group, merge, reshape and window tabular data, comparing each operation with its plain-Python equivalent.
topics.description: pandas adds labelled rows and columns on top of NumPy. You start with a single labelled column (Series), then build and read tables, select and derive columns, handle missing values, sort, group, merge, clean text, work with dates, resample, pivot, bin and compute rolling features. Group-by and merge lessons first solve the task with dictionaries so the library's behaviour is not magic. Packages: pandas and numpy. Packs are validated on pandas 2.2 (the executor image) and pandas 3.x; code avoids chained assignment so it behaves the same under Copy-on-Write. Project ideas: ungraded briefs between steps suggest things to build with what you have learned so far.

topics.title: FastAPI
topics.outcome: Understand HTTP messages, URLs, JSON and routing by hand, then build, validate, secure, run asynchronously and test FastAPI services.
topics.description: Web APIs from first principles. The first half uses only the standard library: the structure of HTTP requests and responses, status codes, URLs and query strings, JSON bodies, a hand-made router, asyncio, and a minimal ASGI application. The second half rebuilds the same ideas with FastAPI — routes, typed parameters and validation, Pydantic request bodies, error handling, response models, dependencies, asynchronous endpoints — and finishes by writing API tests. Packages: standard library for steps 1–7; fastapi (with httpx, used by fastapi.testclient.TestClient) from step 8. No server is started and no network is used: tests call the application in-process, and external services are replaced by fakes. Prerequisite: the Python topic only; you can take this topic any time after Python. Project ideas: ungraded briefs between steps suggest things to build with what you have learned so far.

topics.title: Machine Learning
topics.outcome: Build baselines and core models by hand, then use scikit-learn's estimator API, splits, pipelines, ColumnTransformer, cross-validation, grid search, trees, random forests, gradient boosting, ROC/PR thresholds and k-means in an end-to-end project.
topics.description: Machine learning from the ground up, then with scikit-learn. You start with features, labels and baselines, then learn the estimator API (fit, predict, score, clone), splitting, classification metrics and scaling inside a pipeline. Least squares, gradient-descent regression and logistic regression are built by hand; k-NN, validation curves, cross-validation, ColumnTransformer pipelines, regularisation with grid search, decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, ROC and precision–recall thresholds and k-means use scikit-learn. A capstone combines everything in one leak-free workflow. Packages: numpy, pandas and scikit-learn. Where a library step replaces an earlier from-scratch step, that step follows it as an optional deep dive showing what the library does inside. Project ideas: a house-price predictor, a spam or fraud classifier, and serving your model with FastAPI.

topics.title: Deep Learning
topics.outcome: Understand neurons, activations, losses, backpropagation and optimisers in NumPy, then build, train, debug, save and reproduce PyTorch models with nn.Module, autograd, torch.optim, DataLoader, dropout, batch normalisation and Conv1d.
topics.description: Neural networks in two passes. In NumPy you write activations, softmax, cross-entropy, dense layers, a tiny scalar autograd engine and backpropagation, and SGD with momentum. In PyTorch you then use tensors, nn.Module, autograd, custom gradients with gradcheck, torch.optim, Dataset and DataLoader, a full training loop, dropout, batch normalisation and Conv1d, and finish with saving, loading, reproducibility and debugging training. Packages: numpy, then torch (CPU). Everything trains in about a second. The NumPy versions of the MLP, gradient check, Adam, XOR training, dropout, batch normalisation and convolution stay as optional deep dives after their PyTorch steps. Project ideas: a handwritten digit recogniser and a training-diagnostics notebook.

topics.title: Computer Vision
topics.outcome: Treat images as arrays, then process them with OpenCV (colour spaces, transforms, thresholds, histograms, edges, resizing, contours, connected components), train a small PyTorch CNN with augmentation, and post-process detections with IoU and NMS.
topics.description: Images are arrays of numbers. After image dtypes and colour-to-grey conversion, OpenCV takes over: BGR order and indexing, flips, rotations and affine warps, thresholding with Otsu's method, histograms and equalisation, 2D filtering, Sobel and Canny edges, PSNR, resizing, contours and bounding boxes. With PyTorch you use pooling layers and a convolution layer, train a small CNN and add data augmentation; the topic ends with IoU, non-maximum suppression and connected components. Packages: numpy, opencv-python-headless and torch. Images are small synthetic arrays defined in the tests. The NumPy versions of the library steps follow them as optional deep dives. Project ideas: a document scanner, a shape and colour sorter, and an object counter.

topics.title: Natural Language Processing
topics.outcome: Clean and tokenise text, count and vectorise it with CountVectorizer and TF-IDF, retrieve documents, compare strings, classify text with scikit-learn pipelines and error analysis, and learn word embeddings with PPMI and PyTorch.
topics.description: Working with text: regular expressions, tokenisation and normalisation, word and character n-gram counts with Counter and CountVectorizer, bag-of-words vectors, TF-IDF and cosine-similarity search with scikit-learn, edit distance, Naive Bayes, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression text classifier with error analysis, PPMI word vectors and analogies, and learned embeddings with PyTorch's nn.EmbeddingBag. Packages: standard library, numpy, scikit-learn and torch. The hand-written stopword, character n-gram and retrieval steps, bigram counts and the suffix stemmer are optional deep dives. Project ideas: a review sentiment analyser and semantic search for the club blog.

topics.title: Large Language Models
topics.outcome: Map text to tokens, model and decode next tokens, build attention and transformer blocks, train a tiny GPT in PyTorch, and build LangChain prompts, structured output and RAG pipelines with citation checks.
topics.description: How a language model turns text into tokens and tokens into text: vocabularies and token IDs, next-token probabilities, temperature, greedy decoding and perplexity, byte-pair encoding, then the transformer — scaled dot-product attention, causal masks, positional encodings, multi-head attention and a pre-norm block as a PyTorch nn.Module — then sampling (top-k/top-p), beam search, KV caching and a tiny character-level GPT trained in PyTorch. The topic ends with LangChain: chat prompts and messages, structured output with Pydantic and retries, and retrieval-augmented generation with citation checks. Packages: numpy, torch and langchain-core. No model weights are downloaded and no API is called: LangChain steps use fake chat models, so tests are exact. The NumPy transformer block, the hand-made chat template and RAG pipeline are optional deep dives. Project ideas: a poem or name generator, a course FAQ chatbot and a prompt playground.

topics.title: Explainable AI
topics.outcome: Explain models with contributions, decision paths, ICE curves, scikit-learn partial dependence and permutation importance, occlusion, surrogates, Shapley values, LIME, counterfactuals and integrated gradients.
topics.description: Explaining predictions, from models that explain themselves (linear contributions, decision paths) to model-agnostic methods — ICE curves, partial dependence and permutation importance with sklearn.inspection, occlusion, global surrogates, exact Shapley values, LIME, counterfactuals — and a gradient method for neural networks (integrated gradients). Every model being explained is small and defined in the test, so each attribution can be checked. Packages: numpy, pandas and scikit-learn. The NumPy partial dependence and permutation importance are optional deep dives. Project idea: explain your house-price model.

topics.title: Federated Learning
topics.outcome: Simulate clients and partitions, train client copies of PyTorch models, aggregate state_dicts with weighted FedAvg, and add client sampling, clipping, secure aggregation, differential privacy and FedProx.
topics.description: Training a model across many clients without collecting their data. The topic simulates clients in one process: IID and label-skewed partitions, weighted averaging, client updates as deltas, client training of a PyTorch model copy, a FedAvg round and full training loop, FedAvg over PyTorch state_dicts, client sampling, update clipping, secure aggregation with pairwise masks, differentially private aggregation and FedProx. Packages: numpy and torch. The privacy steps teach the mechanics (clipping, noise, masking); they do not compute formal privacy guarantees. Local SGD in NumPy is an optional deep dive. Project idea: federated training across departments, with a pointer to the Flower framework.

topics.title: Reinforcement Learning
topics.outcome: Define environments and returns (including Gymnasium environments), explore with bandits, solve MDPs with dynamic programming, and learn values with Monte Carlo, TD(0), Q-learning on FrozenLake and SARSA.
topics.description: Learning from rewards. You first define returns, a gridworld transition function and the reset/step environment interface — then the same environment as a real gymnasium.Env with spaces and a time-limit wrapper. You explore with ε-greedy, incremental estimates and UCB bandits, solve known MDPs with policy evaluation, value iteration and policy iteration, and learn from experience with first-visit Monte Carlo, TD(0), Q-learning (also on Gymnasium's FrozenLake) and SARSA. Packages: numpy and gymnasium. MDP format (design choice): P[s][a] is a list of (probability, next_state, reward, done) tuples; terminal transitions stop bootstrapping. All environments are tiny and seeded, so every result is reproducible. Project ideas: a grid game agent and a bandit-based recommender.

topics.title: Agentic AI
topics.outcome: Build agent loops, parsing, budgets, ReAct, planners and evaluation by hand, then LangChain tools and LangGraph graphs with tool nodes, checkpointed memory, validated retries, orchestrator–workers and human-approval guardrails.
topics.description: Agents are programs that repeatedly decide on an action, act through tools and observe the result. You first build each part with ordinary Python and a scripted model — tool registries, parsing model output, perceive–act loops, goals and budgets, the ReAct loop, BFS and A* planners, dependency-ordered plans and an evaluation harness. Then you use the libraries: LangChain tools and tool calling, LangGraph state graphs, a ReAct agent with a tool node and checkpointed threads, message trimming, validated tool arguments with retries, orchestrator–workers with Send, and human approval with interrupts. Packages: standard library, langchain-core and langgraph. Fake chat models keep every test deterministic; no paid API or network is used. The hand-written memory window, validate-and-retry, orchestrator and guardrail steps are optional deep dives. Project ideas: a study-planner agent, a club event assistant and an agent evaluation suite.
